sections.html:
Anything offered for the public record in La Paz County is filed with this office. That includes real property transactions, mortgages, family trusts, tax liens, mining notices, survey maps and military discharges. The office sits in Parker, the county seat, and also runs voter registration and early voting.

Records are kept on microfilm to archival standards, and images of recorded documents from 1983 to the present can be viewed and printed online. A public workstation in the office does the same. Documents arrive by mail, in person, or by electronic recording through a trusted submitter. Call 928-669-6136, or look on the county website for the Recorded Document Search page and the Forms page.

La Paz County takes paper documents that follow the layout rules on its Document Recording Information page. A paper that misses a state requirement is sent back unrecorded, and so is one that arrives without the right fees. Staff cannot help you prepare a document.

Document elementLa Paz County rule
Paper size8.5 inches wide, no shorter than 11 and no longer than 14 inches
First page top margin2 inches; the left 3.5 inches holds the return name and address and the right 3.5 inches is reserved for the Recorder
Other marginsAt least 1/2 inch
Print10-point type or larger, in black and white, except blue ink signatures or color notary stamps
TitleA title on the first page
SignaturesOriginal ink signatures
Amendments or releasesState the date and instrument number of the document being modified

A.R.S. 11-480 holds the full list. After accepting your document, the office indexes it and either mails the original to the address typed on it or hands it back at the counter to walk-in filers.

Most deeds cannot be recorded without this form. A.R.S. 11-1133 has the buyer and seller, or their agents, complete it on a Department of Revenue form. A deed with an incomplete affidavit and no exemption note must be refused by the recorder. Every sale requires either the affidavit or an exemption number, and the Arizona Department of Revenue, at 602-716-6843, answers questions about it.

Four things are on the county's Forms page: the affidavit, a list of exempt codes, the fee schedule PDF and a recording cover sheet.

  • Under A.R.S. 11-1134, exempt transfers include gifts, quitclaim deeds given for no money, court-ordered conveyances, and deeds that confirm or correct an earlier recorded deed.
  • Token-price transfers among spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, or siblings qualify as well.
  • The list also covers a trustee's deed under a power of sale, a nominal-consideration transfer into or out of a trust, and a transfer creating joint tenancy with right of survivorship.
  • When recording an exempt deed, write the specific exemption on its face.

Recording a single instrument costs $30 by state law, and $15 if a government body is a party and requests the recording. Section 11-475 of the statutes notes that both amounts include the charge under 11-475.01.

Each copied page is $1, and a certified copy adds $3 for the recorder's certificate and seal. Mail requests need a self-addressed stamped envelope plus the instrument number. Questions about fees can go to the posted fee schedule or to the office at 928-669-6136.

Send too little and the whole package comes back unrecorded. Let your title company confirm the amount with the Recorder before the deed leaves, and make sure the same figure appears on your settlement statement.

No new one can be created. Article 9, Section 24 of the Arizona Constitution stops the state, counties, cities and districts from imposing a fresh tax, fee, stamp requirement or other assessment on the sale or transfer of real property, with a carve-out for charges that were already in place on December 31, 2007.

What matters at your closing is the list of charges on the statement. Recording is one of them. The affidavit is a reporting form that helps the assessor and the Department of Revenue follow sales. Ask the title company to break out everything related to recording, then check it against the county fee schedule.

Search the document images online, or have a title company run a search. Common needs have specific routes:

  • A sale price: search the images and choose the document type affidavit of property value.
  • Prior owners: search the grantor and grantee name index, or order a title search.
  • An owner's name for a parcel: call the County Assessor at 928-669-6165.
  • A subdivision plat: ask the Recorder in person or by mail, with the map book and page number from the deed.

Certified or plain copies of any recorded document can be requested by instrument number, in person or by mail.

sections.h2: From closing table to recorded deed
sections.html:
Here is how a typical sale moves through this office.

  1. You and the buyer sign the deed in original ink, and the affidavit of property value is finished or an exemption code is chosen.
  2. Escrow gathers the recording fee and the cover sheet.
  3. The title company sends the deed to Parker by mail, in person or electronically through a trusted submitter.
  4. Staff check it against the layout rules, then index it so it can be searched by name.
  5. The original goes to the return address typed on the document, or into your hands at the counter.

Nobody at the office will draft or fix a deed for you, so a title company or attorney should review the paper before it goes. If the house sat empty or came to you through a family transfer, search the index for older recorded papers before you list, so nothing surprises the buyer's title company. A cash sale keeps the list shorter because no lender needs recorded documents of its own, but the deed, the affidavit and the fee are still required.

Voters carved La Paz County out of northern Yuma County on January 1, 1983, making it the only Arizona county formed after statehood. Its 4,514 square miles run along the Colorado River on the state's western edge. Parker holds the county seat, Quartzsite is the second incorporated place, and the Colorado River Indian Reservation occupies the western part.

About 16,711 people live here, in 13,783 housing units, and the 2020 census found 45.2 percent of units vacant. The median owner-occupied home was valued at $135,800 for 2020 through 2024. Owners occupy 72.1 percent of occupied homes, 38.6 percent of residents are 65 or older, and median household income was $49,478.

faqs.q: What is the phone number for the La Paz County Recorder?
faqs.a: Call 928-669-6136. That is the number listed for fee questions.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in La Paz County?
faqs.a: State law charges $30 for each instrument and $15 for a government requester. Review the county's fee schedule PDF before mailing, since an underpaid package comes back unrecorded.

faqs.q: Can I record documents electronically in La Paz County?
faqs.a: Yes, through a trusted submitter. The office also takes documents by mail and in person.

faqs.q: How far back are La Paz County recorded documents online?
faqs.a: Images of recorded documents from 1983 to the present can be viewed and printed online. A public workstation in the office offers the same access.

faqs.q: What happens if my document does not meet the requirements?
faqs.a: It comes back to you unrecorded, as do papers sent without the correct fees. The office cannot help you prepare the document.
